it-2007-cs-45.approach: A stuck-at-0 fault on T is detected only by an input that (1) drives T to 1 in the good circuit and (2) lets the value of T reach the output. Write the output in terms of T and check both conditions together.

steps.title: Output expression
steps.body:
Let $N = \overline{X_1X_2X_3}$ (the NAND) and $T = X_3X_4$ (the AND). The OR gate gives $N + X_4$, and the NOR gives
$$F = \overline{(N + X_4) + T}.$$

steps.title: Activate the fault
steps.body: With $T$ grounded the faulty line is always 0. The good and faulty circuits can differ only if the good value of $T$ is 1, i.e. $X_3 = X_4 = 1$.

steps.title: Propagate the fault
steps.body: For $F$ to depend on $T$, the other NOR input $N + X_4$ must be 0. That needs $X_4 = 0$, which contradicts activation ($X_4 = 1$). With $X_4 = 1$ the NOR has a 1 input, so $F = 0$ whatever $T$ is.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: No input vector both activates and propagates the fault, so the fault is undetectable and the answer is **None of the above**.

answer.value: None of the above (the fault is undetectable)

optionAnalysis.reason: 0000: good $T = 0$, which equals the stuck value, so the fault is not activated. Both circuits give $F = 0$ because $N = 1$.
0111: $T = 1$ activates the fault, but $X_4 = 1$ forces the OR output to 1, so $F = 0$ in both circuits.
1111: $N = 0$, but $X_4 = 1$ still makes the OR output 1, so $F = 0$ with or without the fault.
Activation needs $X_4 = 1$ and propagation needs $X_4 = 0$, so no test vector exists.

it-2007-cs-45.shortcut: $X_4$ feeds both $T$ (through the AND) and the other NOR input (through the OR). The fault needs $X_4 = 1$, and that same 1 masks it at the NOR.
pitfalls: Choosing an input that makes T = 1 without checking that the change reaches the output.
The exact NAND inputs do not matter: the masking comes from X4 alone.
it-2007-cs-45.verification: Evaluated all three listed vectors in the good and faulty circuits: the outputs agree each time (F = 0).

it-2007-cs-46.approach: Read off what each grammar can generate: G1 switches from an x/z part to a y/z part with no way back, and G2 can only produce x through S → xB, after which B must emit y.

steps.title: Language of G1
steps.body: S produces any string of $x$ and $z$ ($xS$, $zS$) and may end with $x$ or $z$, or switch to $yB$. B produces only $y$ and $z$ ($yB$, $zB$, $y$, $z$) and never returns to S. So $L(G_1) \subseteq (x+z)^*\,(\varepsilon + y(y+z)^*)$: once a $y$ appears, no $x$ can follow. In other words, **no $y$ appears before any $x$**.

steps.title: Language of G2
steps.body: The only rule that makes an $x$ is $S \to xB$, and $B \to y \mid yS$ always emits $y$ next. So **every $x$ is immediately followed by a $y$**, which means every $x$ is followed by at least one $y$.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: G1: no y appears before any x. G2: every x is followed by at least one y. This is option A.

answer.value: G1: no y appears before any x; G2: every x is followed by at least one y

optionAnalysis.reason: Both statements match the derivations above.
G2 allows an x before a y, e.g. $S \Rightarrow xB \Rightarrow xy$, so 'no x appears before any y' fails for G2.
G1 allows a y after an x: $S \Rightarrow xS \Rightarrow xyB \Rightarrow xyy$.
The G1 part fails as in C, and G2 generates $y$ alone, where the y is not followed by any x.

pitfalls: 'No y before any x' and 'no y after any x' are different conditions. G1 forbids x after y, which is the first one.
it-2007-cs-46.verification: Checked the counterexamples xy (G2) and xyy (G1) by explicit derivation.

steps.body:
expr derives only ID, and stmnt → WHILE ( expr ) stmnt is tail recursion, so
$$L(G_1) = (\texttt{WHILE ( ID )})^*\ \texttt{OTHER},$$
a regular expression. (The parentheses are terminals and appear as a flat pair around a single expr, so no unbounded nesting has to be matched.)

steps.title: Grammar G2
steps.body:
expr → expr + expr | expr * expr | ID derives $\texttt{ID}((+ \mid *)\,\texttt{ID})^*$, which is regular even though the grammar is ambiguous and not right-linear. Then
$$L(G_2) = (\texttt{WHILE (}\ E\ \texttt{)})^*\ \texttt{OTHER},\quad E = \texttt{ID}((+\mid *)\texttt{ID})^*,$$
also regular.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both are context-free grammars whose languages are regular, so both G1 and G2 are regular: option C.

answer.value: Both G1 and G2 are regular

optionAnalysis.reason: G1's language is $(\texttt{WHILE ( ID )})^*\texttt{OTHER}$, which is regular.
G2's expressions $\texttt{ID}((+\mid *)\texttt{ID})^*$ are regular, so G2 is regular too.
Both languages have regular expressions.
Neither language needs matching of unbounded nesting, so both are regular.

steps.title: Throughput
steps.body:
Each 1000-byte burst occupies $800 + 80 = 880\ \mu s$:
$$\text{Throughput} = \frac{8000 \text{ bits}}{880\ \mu s} = \frac{100}{11} \text{ Mbps} \approx 9.09 \text{ Mbps}.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 1 Mbps is the capacity split equally among the 10 nodes, which ignores that only one node transmits at a time.
Efficiency $800/880 = 10/11$ of 10 Mbps.
10 Mbps ignores the polling overhead.
Throughput can never exceed the 10 Mbps channel capacity.

it-2007-cs-65.approach: Under a uniform distribution, the selectivity of A ≤ v is (v − min)/(max − min). Multiply by the number of tuples.

steps.title: Estimate
steps.body: $$1000 \times \frac{1}{5} = 200 \text{ tuples}.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 50 would be a selectivity of 1/20.
100 confuses the bound A ≤ 100 with the number of tuples.
150 does not follow from a uniform distribution.

it-2007-cs-65.verification: One fifth of the value range holds one fifth of the 1000 tuples.

it-2007-cs-66.approach: Strict 2PL: the transaction must lock before access (shared to read, exclusive to write), never lock after its first unlock, and hold every exclusive lock until it commits. Shared locks may be released earlier.

steps.title: Lock types needed
steps.body: T1 reads A and writes B, so it needs S(A) and X(B). T2 reads B and writes A, so it needs S(B) and X(A). Any X lock must be released only after commit.

steps.title: Eliminate
steps.body:
**A:** writes B under only lockS(B) (and A under lockS(A)): a write without an exclusive lock, so invalid.

**B:** S1 takes lockX(A) and releases it before commit. An exclusive lock released before commit breaks strictness.

**D:** both schedules release their X lock (B in S1, A in S2) before commit: not strict.

steps.title: Option C
steps.body: S1: lockS(A), lockX(B), …, unlock(A); commit; unlock(B). The X lock on B is held until after commit, and the early release of the shared lock on A is allowed, so S1 is strict 2PL. S2 is the mirror image (lockS(B), lockX(A)). Its intended order is unlock(B); commit; unlock(A). The scan prints unlock(A) before commit, which would release the X lock early, apparently a transcription slip. The intended answer is C.

optionAnalysis.reason: Writes B (and A) while holding only shared locks.
Releases an exclusive lock, X(A) in S1, before commit.
Correct lock modes; exclusive locks are held until commit (S2 as intended, mirroring S1).
Releases the exclusive locks before commit.

pitfalls: Strict 2PL restricts only exclusive locks; shared locks may be released before commit.
Rigorous 2PL (all locks held to commit) is stricter than what is asked.
it-2007-cs-66.verification: Checked the lock mode used for each write and the position of each X-unlock relative to commit, in all four options.
